title: US Ends Duration of Status for Student Visas Starting September 15
excerpt: International students, including over 360,000 Indians enrolled at US universities, face fixed admission periods, shorter grace periods, and new extension requirements under the DHS overhaul.
body:
• Starting September 15, 2026, the US replaces the decades-old "Duration of Status" system with fixed admission periods capped at four years for F-1, J-1, and I visa holders.
  • The post-completion grace period is being cut from 60 days to 30 days, giving students less time to depart, transfer, or arrange OPT after finishing their programs.
  • Students needing more than four years must now apply to USCIS for an Extension of Stay, undergo biometric verification, and pay additional fees — a process previously handled by universities.
  • Current students already in the US will automatically transition to the new framework, with their stay capped at four years from the rule's effective date.

The US Department of Homeland Security is implementing one of the most significant changes to student immigration rules in decades. Starting September 15, 2026, the longstanding "Duration of Status" framework that allowed international students to remain in the country for as long as they maintained valid enrollment will be replaced with fixed admission periods.

The final rule, published in the Federal Register on July 17, affects F-1 student visas, J-1 exchange visitor visas, and I visas for foreign media representatives. There is no grace period for the transition — the changes take effect on the date specified, regardless of when students enrolled.

What Changes on September 15

Under the previous system, international students could remain in the US indefinitely as long as they maintained valid student status and complied with visa rules. Universities managed extensions through the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), without requiring federal approval.

The new rule replaces this flexibility with a fixed "admit until" date on Form I-94, based on the program end date listed on Form I-20, subject to a maximum of four years. Students receive a 30-day arrival period before classes begin and a 30-day departure period after completing their studies — down from the previous 60-day departure window.

Extension Process Shifts to Federal Control

Students whose programs extend beyond four years — common for doctoral candidates, postdoctoral researchers, and medical trainees — must now apply to USCIS by filing Form I-539, paying required fees, and completing biometric verification including background checks and fraud screenings.

"For decades, foreign students have been admitted into the US indefinitely, allowing thousands to abuse our immigration system by perpetually enrolling in courses to avoid having to leave."

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

Alternatively, students with valid visas may leave the US and seek readmission with a new admission period based on updated SEVIS records. Neither extension nor readmission is guaranteed.

Impact on Indian Students

The changes are particularly significant for Indian students, who now form the largest international student community in the United States. More than 360,000 Indians were enrolled at American universities during the 2024-25 academic year, many pursuing master's, doctoral, and STEM programs that frequently extend beyond four years.

The rule also affects Optional Practical Training. While the OPT program itself remains unchanged — allowing 12 months of standard work authorization and a 24-month STEM extension — students must now ensure their underlying F-1 admission remains valid throughout the OPT period.

Transition Rules for Current Students

Students already in the US under Duration of Status will automatically convert to a fixed admission period. Their end date will be the later of their program end date on Form I-20 or their EAD expiration date, but capped at no more than four years from September 15, 2026. The legacy 60-day grace period is preserved for this transition group.

Students with pending or soon-to-be-filed OPT or STEM OPT applications as of September 15 — or filed before March 18, 2027 — will not be required to file a separate Extension of Stay application.

Several American universities have reportedly advised international students currently outside the country to return before September 15 to avoid complications during the transition to the new system. The rule arrives alongside other immigration measures this year, including increased H-1B premium processing fees and a proposed 30% raise in minimum wage requirements for H-1B workers.
